request:
Hey, SL Computer Science. Source A below is the bit of my IA development write-up where I justify writing my own sort for my leaderboard app (it's a Python project but I've written the algorithm in IB pseudocode like we're supposed to). My teacher handed it back with "trace it", "check your maths" and "source?" written next to the bit about Knuth, and that's all the feedback I got. Can you:

1. Trace my SORT procedure by hand on A = [7, 3, 9, 1, 5] (so N = 5), showing the array after every pass of the outer loop and how many comparisons and swaps happen. Does it actually work as written? If something's wrong, show me exactly which line and what the fix is, don't just rewrite the whole thing.
2. Check my complexity claim against my timing table with actual working. What does the data say the growth rate is, and what would the time really be for the 100 000-player leaderboard I mention? Also is the "O(n) when nearly sorted" claim correct?
3. Go through every claim in Source A and tell me which ones are justified, which are wrong, and which are just unsupported, including the history bit about Knuth and the bit about real languages using bubble sort. If you cite something, say what it is and how sure you are, because my teacher checks.
4. Give me a provisional mark for this section against the Development criterion (12 marks in the rubric we were given) and say what would move it up.

Please don't rewrite the section for me, I'm not allowed to submit anything I didn't write myself, I just need to understand what's wrong.

supplied_texts.title: Source A: IA development write-up extract, section 3.2 (student's own draft)
supplied_texts.text:
3.2 Choosing and justifying the sorting algorithm

The leaderboard screen must show players in descending order of score. I decided to write my own sorting algorithm rather than calling Python's built-in sort() so that I could demonstrate my understanding of algorithms. Bubble sort is the fastest algorithm for small lists, which is why real programming languages use it inside their built-in sort functions anyway, so there is no loss of performance.

SORT(A)   // A is an array of scores indexed 0 to N-1
  loop I from 0 to N-1
    SWAPPED = false
    loop J from 0 to N-1-I
      if A[J] > A[J+1] then
        TEMP = A[J]
        A[J] = A[J+1]
        A[J+1] = TEMP
        SWAPPED = true
      end if
    end loop
    if SWAPPED = false then
      break
    end if
  end loop
end SORT

Because of the SWAPPED flag the algorithm stops early, which makes it O(n) for nearly sorted data (which the leaderboard usually is, since only one score changes at a time) and O(n log n) on average. Big O notation was invented by Donald Knuth in 1976 specifically for comparing sorting algorithms.

I tested SORT on random lists of scores in Python (average of three runs):

Table 3. Timing results
n = 1 000 -> 0.052 s
n = 2 000 -> 0.21 s
n = 4 000 -> 0.85 s
n = 8 000 -> 3.4 s

When n doubles the time grows a bit faster than double, which is consistent with O(n log n). Extrapolating, the school's planned 100 000-player leaderboard would sort in well under a second, so the algorithm is suitable.

strong_answer_must: Spot the off-by-one bug: with 'loop J from 0 to N-1-I' (inclusive, as IB pseudocode loops are), the first pass (I = 0) runs J up to N-1 = 4 and compares A[4] with A[5], which does not exist; in Python this raises an index error, in pseudocode it is undefined. The fix is to change the inner bound to N-2-I (or stop the outer loop one earlier and keep J < N-1-I); the answer must name the line and not rewrite the whole procedure.

Trace with the corrected bound on [7, 3, 9, 1, 5]: after pass 1 [3, 7, 1, 5, 9] (4 comparisons, 3 swaps); after pass 2 [3, 1, 5, 7, 9] (3 comparisons, 2 swaps); after pass 3 [1, 3, 5, 7, 9] (2 comparisons, 1 swap); pass 4 makes 1 comparison and no swap, so SWAPPED = false and the loop breaks. Totals: 10 comparisons, 6 swaps, 4 passes (3 with swaps).

Point out that the procedure sorts ascending (larger values move to the end) while the leaderboard is specified as descending order of score, so either the comparison must be '<' or the list must be reversed; this is a mismatch between the stated requirement and the code.

Compute the timing ratios: 0.21/0.052 ≈ 4.0, 0.85/0.21 ≈ 4.0, 3.4/0.85 = 4.0, i.e. doubling n quadruples the time, and/or the log-log slope log(3.4/0.052)/log(8) ≈ 2.0; both indicate Θ(n^2), not n log n. State that for n log n a doubling from 1000 to 2000 would give a ratio of about 2.2, so 'a bit faster than double' does not describe a factor of 4.

Predict the 100 000-player time: 3.4 s × (100 000/8 000)^2 ≈ 530 s ≈ 9 minutes; and note that even on the student's own n log n assumption it would be about 54 s, so 'well under a second' is wrong on either model. Mention that extrapolating a factor of 12.5 beyond the measured range is itself an assumption (memory effects, but the direction of the conclusion is robust).

Correct the complexity claims: bubble sort with an early-exit flag is O(n) only when the input is already sorted (one pass of n-1 comparisons); average and worst case are Θ(n^2) (a random permutation has about n(n-1)/4 inversions and bubble sort removes one per swap). For 'only one score changes', explain the rabbit/turtle asymmetry: an element that must move towards the end moves in one pass, but one that must move towards the front moves one place per pass, so the cost can be O(k·n) for a move of k places; a single insertion into a sorted list is O(n) with insertion (or binary search + shift), which is the better justification.

Correct the history, hedged as recalled: Big O notation is due to Paul Bachmann (1894, 'Analytische Zahlentheorie') and was popularised by Edmund Landau (1909); it was not invented for comparing sorting algorithms. Donald Knuth's 1976 SIGACT News note 'Big Omicron and big Omega and big Theta' standardised the use of Ω and Θ in algorithm analysis, which is probably where the student's '1976' comes from. The answer must say where this comes from (recalled knowledge) and not invent page numbers or quotations.

Correct 'real languages use bubble sort inside their built-in sort': Python's sorted()/list.sort uses Timsort (Tim Peters, 2002, Python 2.3), a merge/insertion hybrid that uses binary insertion sort for short runs (minrun around 32-64); Java's Arrays.sort uses Timsort for objects (since Java 7, 2011) and dual-pivot quicksort (Yaroslavskiy) for primitives, with insertion sort below a small threshold; none use bubble sort. Insertion sort, not bubble sort, is the usual small-n choice; Knuth (The Art of Computer Programming vol. 3) and Astrachan's 2003 SIGCSE paper on bubble sort both conclude it has little to recommend it. Thresholds and dates to be hedged.

Classify each claim: 'must show descending order' (requirement, fine but not met by the code); 'wrote own sort to demonstrate understanding' (acceptable rationale, but should acknowledge the built-in is faster and O(n log n) worst case); 'bubble sort is fastest for small lists' (wrong/unsupported); 'real languages use it' (wrong); 'O(n) for nearly sorted' (only partly true, see above); 'O(n log n) on average' (wrong); 'Knuth 1976' (misattributed); 'data consistent with n log n' (contradicted by the data); 'well under a second' (contradicted by the data).

Note methodological gaps in the test: no statement of the range of random scores, what was timed (sort only or list generation too), hardware, or the variance of the three runs; recommend a plot of log t against log n and a comparison run against the built-in sort at the same n.

Give a provisional Development mark with a hedge (e.g. in the region of 4-6 out of 12 as it stands, because there is an algorithm and testing but the algorithm is buggy, the complexity reasoning is wrong and claims are unsupported) and say concretely what would raise it: a corrected and traced algorithm, an honest Θ(n^2) analysis with the measured evidence, a justified comparison with the built-in sort, and correctly attributed sources. The mark must be labelled provisional in the same sentence.

Respect the boundary: explain what is wrong and how to check it, without rewriting section 3.2 for submission; include a single Sources line tagged per the shared rules (e.g. 'recalled, not consulted' for Bachmann/Landau/Knuth, Timsort and Java sort details).
pitfalls: Tracing the procedure 'as written' to a sorted result without noticing that J reaches N-1 and A[J+1] is out of range on the very first pass; or claiming the bug is elsewhere (e.g. in the outer loop bound, which is harmless).
A trace with wrong intermediate arrays (e.g. after pass 1 giving [3, 7, 1, 9, 5], which stops the pass one comparison early) or miscounted comparisons/swaps.
Accepting the n log n claim, or saying the data 'cannot determine' the growth rate when three consecutive ratios of 4.0 clearly indicate n^2.
Arithmetic slips in the extrapolation (e.g. 3.4 × 12.5 = 42.5 s treated as the quadratic prediction, or 531 s reported as 'about 53 s').
Agreeing that an early-exit bubble sort is O(n) for 'nearly sorted' data in general, or claiming its average case is O(n log n).

Fabricated attribution: confirming 'Knuth 1976' as the inventor of Big O, attributing it to Landau alone, inventing a paper title or journal volume, or quoting Knuth's 'catchy name' remark as verbatim certain text without a hedge.
Claiming Python or Java use quicksort or bubble sort in their built-in sort, stating exact insertion-sort thresholds as certain, or inventing a version number.
Awarding a mark without labelling it provisional, awarding a high mark despite the bug, or rewriting the section wholesale for the student.
